items.p: Sort these. Do they dissolve in water or not?
items.a: see items
items.why: Things that dissolve leave the water clear, even if coloured. Things that do not dissolve sink, float or make the water cloudy.

items.p: A thing that can dissolve in water is called ____.
items.why: Soluble means it can dissolve. Insoluble means it cannot.

items.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3, stirs a spoon of atta into water. The water turns white and cloudy. What will happen if she leaves it still for an hour?
opts: It will turn clear and the atta will be gone
Most of the atta will settle on the bottom
items.why: Atta does not dissolve. Its tiny bits float for a while, then settle on the bottom. Cloudy water is a sign that something has not dissolved.

items.p: When salt dissolves, it is gone from the water.
items.why: False. The salt is still there, in particles too small to see. You can taste it, and you get it back when the water dries up.

items.p: You cannot see the salt in a glass of salt water. Write two ways to show that the salt is still there.
items.a: Taste a drop: it is salty. Leave the water in the sun until it dries: salt crystals are left behind.
items.why: A strong answer gives two different tests and says what each one would show.

items.p: Match each word to what it means.
pairs: mix into a liquid and disappear from sight
a liquid with something dissolved in it
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: These four words come up all through the unit.

items.p: In the Full Glass Test, three tablespoons of water got two or three teaspoons of salt. Then grains stayed on the bottom. What does this show?
opts: The water could not dissolve any more salt
items.why: The water had reached its limit for salt. It was saturated. The salt was the same salt that had dissolved a minute before.

items.p: Draw two glasses. In one, draw salt water. In the other, draw rava in water. Show what you would see.
items.a: Salt water drawn clear, with nothing on the bottom. Rava water with grains lying on the bottom and clear water above.
items.why: A good drawing shows that dissolved salt cannot be seen, but rava stays as grains.
items.art: Two empty glass outlines side by side.

items.p: Which one is the odd one out?
items.why: Oil does not dissolve in water. It floats as a layer. Salt, sugar and jaggery all dissolve.

items.p: A cloth or a tea strainer that catches bits but lets liquid through is called a ____.
items.why: A filter catches things that have not dissolved, like tea leaves. Dissolved things go through it.

items.p: Which glass dissolves a spoon of sugar fastest?
items.why: In warm water the water particles move faster. They knock sugar particles off the grains faster.

items.p: Arjun, a boy in Class 2, says, 'The tea strainer caught the tea leaves, so it caught the tea too.' What would you tell him?
items.a: The strainer caught only the leaves. The brown colour and the taste of tea dissolved into the water, so they went through the strainer into the cup.
items.why: A strong answer says which part dissolved and which part did not, and that a strainer can catch only what has not dissolved.

items.p: Lemon juice mixes into water completely.
items.why: True. Lemon juice is mostly water with acid and sugars dissolved in it, so it mixes in completely.

items.p: Label this drawing of a glass after the atta test: cloudy water, settled atta, clear water at the top.
items.a: Clear water at the top, cloudy water in the middle, a white layer of settled atta on the bottom.
items.why: When atta settles, the water clears from the top down, and the atta collects at the bottom.
items.art: A tall glass with a clear top part, a cloudy middle and a white layer on the bottom, with three blank label lines.

items.p: Kavya, a girl of nine, and her brother Farhan, who is seven, are making lemonade for their Ammamma. They disagree about the sugar.

views.says: Stir the sugar into a little warm water first. Then add cold water.
Put everything in the cold water and keep stirring. It saves washing another cup.

items.ask: Whose way would you choose? Give a reason from the Cold, Room or Warm test. Then say one good point about the other way.
items.a: A strong answer picks one and uses evidence. For example: Kavya's way, because warm water dissolved sugar in about 20 stirs and cold water took about 90. Then it gives the other side fairly: Farhan's way does work if you stir long enough, and it is simpler.
items.why: Both ways can work. One is faster, and the other is simpler. A good answer weighs both.

items.p: The full salt water still dissolved a spoon of sugar. Explain why, in your own words.
items.a: Water has a separate limit for each thing. Being full of salt does not use up its limit for sugar.
items.why: A strong answer says the limits are separate, not that the water has empty room left.

items.p: Priya, a girl in Class 3, puts 10 spoons of salt in a small cup of water. Some salt stays on the bottom. She stirs for five more minutes. What happens?
opts: The salt on the bottom stays
items.why: Once water is saturated, extra salt stays as grains however long you stir. Stirring only helps water reach its limit faster.

items.p: Put the steps of the Full Glass Test in order.
items: Pour off the clear salt water and add sugar
Put the same water in two glasses
Add salt a spoon at a time and stir
Guess how many spoons each glass will take
a: Put the same water in two glasses
Guess how many spoons each glass will take
Add salt a spoon at a time and stir
Pour off the clear salt water and add sugar
items.why: A fair test starts with the same water, then a guess, then the test, then the extra test with sugar.

items.p: Warm water can dissolve much more salt than cold water.
items.why: False. Warm water dissolves salt a little faster, but it holds only a little more. Sugar is the one that warm water holds much more of.

items.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, strained muddy salty water through a cloth. It came out clear. She says it is now just water. Is she right? Explain.
items.a: No. The cloth caught the mud, but the salt dissolved and went through. The water is still salty. It may still have germs too.
items.why: A strong answer separates what a filter can catch from what has dissolved.

items.p: In the Full Glass Test, Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, did the test. Her salt glass took 3 spoons. Her sugar glass was still going at 10 spoons. How many more spoons did the sugar glass take, at least?
items.why: 10 take away 3 is 7. The sugar glass took at least 7 more spoons, and it could have taken many more.

items.p: Why does oil float on top of water in a bottle, even after you shake it?
opts: Oil dissolves and then comes back
Oil does not dissolve in water, and it is lighter than water
items.why: Oil does not dissolve in water. Its drops join up again and float, because oil is lighter than the same amount of water.

items.p: Draw what you think is happening to a salt grain when it dissolves. Draw the water particles too.
items.a: Water particles around the grain, pulling small salt particles off its outside, and salt particles spread among the water particles.
items.why: A good model shows water particles taking pieces off the outside of the grain and the pieces spreading out.
items.art: A large circle labelled 'zoomed in', empty inside.

items.p: Sort these. Would a cloth filter catch them, or would they go through?
items.a: see items
items.why: A filter catches things that have not dissolved. Dissolved things are too small to catch.

items.p: A solution that cannot dissolve any more of a thing is called ____.
items.why: Saturated means it has reached its limit for that thing.

items.p: Nandini, a girl in Class 4, makes coffee with filter coffee powder. What is left in the filter?
opts: The coffee grounds, which did not dissolve
items.why: Hot water dissolves the colour and flavour out of the powder. The rest of the powder does not dissolve and stays in the filter.

items.p: A cook makes sugar syrup by heating sugar and water together. Why does she heat it?
items.a: Hot water can dissolve much more sugar than cold water, and it dissolves faster.
items.why: A strong answer names both reasons: more sugar, and faster.

items.p: Two friends in Class 3, Sunita and Arjun, are arguing about a glass of clear water left after the salt test.

views.says: The water is clear, so the salt has gone.
The salt is still there. We just can't see it.

items.ask: Who do you agree with? Use evidence from your own tests. Then say why the other person's idea makes sense at first.
items.a: A strong answer agrees with Arjun, using evidence: the water tastes salty, and the salt comes back when the water evaporates. It then says that Sunita's idea makes sense at first, because the salt really cannot be seen.
items.why: Seeing is not the only test. Taste and evaporation show the salt is there.

items.p: Label the bottle filter: stones, sand, cotton wool, muddy water going in, clearer water coming out.
items.a: Muddy water at the top, then stones, then sand, then cotton wool in the neck, and clearer water dripping into the glass below.
items.why: The water passes through finer and finer layers, so smaller and smaller bits are caught.
items.art: An upside-down cut bottle with three layers inside and a glass below, with five blank label lines.

items.p: Which one does not make sugar dissolve faster?
items.why: Ice makes the water colder, so the sugar dissolves more slowly. Warm water, stirring and crushing all make it faster.

items.p: Many people think that if you stir long enough, any amount of salt will dissolve. Plan a test to find out if they are right.
items.a: Put three tablespoons of water in a glass. Add salt a spoon at a time until grains stay. Then stir for five more minutes and see if the grains go. Do it twice.
items.why: A strong plan keeps the water the same, adds salt until it stops, then stirs much longer to test the claim.

items.p: Salt water lets electricity through, but sugar water hardly does. What is the reason?
opts: Salt comes apart into charged particles called ions, but sugar stays whole
items.why: Charged ions can carry electricity through water. Sugar molecules have no charge, so sugar water hardly carries electricity.

items.p: Sea water is salty, but the rain that falls on the sea is not. When sea water evaporates, what happens to the salt? Use this to explain how salt pans work.
items.a: Only the water evaporates into the air. The salt stays behind. In salt pans, sea water is let into shallow ponds, the sun evaporates the water, and the salt is left as crystals.
items.why: A strong answer says that the water leaves and the salt stays, and links it to the salt pans.

items.p: Three children in Class 4 explain why the full salt water could still dissolve sugar.

views.says: There was still some empty space in the water.
Water has a different limit for each thing, so salt did not use up the sugar limit.
Sugar is softer than salt, so it squeezed in.

items.ask: Which explanation fits best with all your tests? Give your reason. Then say which part of another explanation could also be true.
items.a: A strong answer picks Meenakshi's, because the sugar glass took more than ten spoons while the salt stopped at three, so each thing has its own limit. It may say Kavya is partly right that dissolved particles fit in among water particles, and that the drink did get bigger.
items.why: The evidence that sugar and salt have different limits in the same water supports separate limits. 'Empty space' and 'softer' do not explain why sugar dissolves so much more.

items.p: 100 millilitres of water dissolves about 36 grams of salt. How much salt would 200 millilitres of water dissolve?
items.why: Twice as much water dissolves twice as much salt. 36 plus 36 is 72 grams.

items.p: Why could Sri Ramakrishna's salt doll dissolve completely in the ocean, when a whole doll in a bucket would not?
opts: The ocean has so much water that it is far below its limit for salt
items.why: How much salt can dissolve depends on how much water there is. A bucket would soon be saturated, and most of the doll would stay on the bottom.

items.p: Svante Arrhenius's examiners thought his idea was wrong. What evidence later showed he was right?
items.a: Salt lowers the freezing point of water about twice as much as the same number of sugar particles, because each bit of salt splits into two ions. And salt solutions carry electricity even when very dilute.
items.why: A strong answer names a measurement that his idea explained and the old idea did not.

items.p: Draw a bar chart of the Full Glass Test: one bar for salt and one bar for sugar, showing how many spoons dissolved.
items.a: A short bar of about 3 for salt and a much taller bar of at least 10 for sugar, with the sugar bar marked 'still going'.
items.why: A good chart shows the big difference at a glance and notes that the sugar limit was not reached.
items.art: Blank axes with 'Spoons' up the side and 'Salt' and 'Sugar' along the bottom.

items.p: A clear glass of water is always safe to drink.
items.why: False. Dissolved things and germs can be in clear water. That is why drinking water is boiled, filtered with special filters or treated.

items.p: Lakshmi, a girl in Class 4, wants to dissolve as much sugar as possible in one cup of water. What should she do?
opts: Use hot water, with a grown-up's help
items.why: Hot water can hold much more sugar than cold water. Boiling water holds more than twice as much.

items.p: Put these in order, from the most sugar that can dissolve in a cup of water to the least.
items.why: The warmer the water, the more sugar it can hold.

items.p: ORS has salt and sugar dissolved in the same water. Using what you found, explain why both can dissolve together.
items.a: Water has a separate limit for salt and for sugar. Dissolving salt does not stop the sugar dissolving, as the full salt water test showed.
items.why: A strong answer links ORS to the evidence from the Full Glass Test.

items.p: Match each thing to what happens to it in water.
pairs: comes apart into two kinds of ions
comes apart into whole sugar molecules
items.a: pairs as given
items.why: Each thing meets water in its own way. Salt and sugar dissolve, but differently. Oil and atta do not dissolve.

items.p: Label the zoomed-in picture of salt water: water particle, sodium ion, chloride ion.
items.a: The many small particles are water. The small charged balls marked plus are sodium ions. The bigger balls marked minus are chloride ions.
items.why: When salt dissolves, its two kinds of particles come apart and spread among the water particles.
items.art: A circle full of small water particles, with a few plus balls and a few bigger minus balls among them, and three blank label lines.

items.p: Sort these. Does heat make a big difference to how much dissolves, or very little?
items.a: see items
items.why: Heat lets water hold much more sugar and jaggery. For salt, the limit hardly changes.

quiz.p: Which of these dissolves in water?
quiz.why: Sugar dissolves and the water goes clear. Sand and rava sink, and oil floats. Picking rava is easy to do because it looks like sugar, but rava is ground wheat, which does not dissolve.

quiz.p: Atta makes water cloudy. What does cloudy water tell you?
opts: Tiny bits of atta are floating and have not dissolved
The water is dirty and must be thrown away
quiz.why: Cloudy water means bits are floating in it. A dissolved thing leaves water clear. If you chose 'dissolved', try leaving the glass for an hour and watch the atta settle.

quiz.p: Meenakshi, a girl in Class 3, stirs salt into water until she cannot see it. Where is the salt?
opts: It is still in the water, in particles too small to see
quiz.why: The salt is still there. You can taste it, and it comes back when the water dries. It has not turned into water: it stays salt.

quiz.p: In the Full Glass Test, which did the same small amount of water dissolve more of?
quiz.why: The water took two or three spoons of salt and more than ten of sugar. Many children guess salt or the same, because the grains look alike.

quiz.p: The salt water was full of salt. Then a spoon of sugar went in. What happened?
opts: The sugar stayed on the bottom
quiz.why: The sugar dissolved, because water has a separate limit for each thing. 'Stayed on the bottom' is what most people guess, because they think 'full' means full of everything.

opts: A solution that cannot dissolve any more of a thing
A solution with oil in it
quiz.why: Saturated means the water has reached its limit for that thing. Extra grains stay on the bottom.

quiz.p: Why does sugar dissolve faster in warm water?
opts: Warm water particles move faster and knock sugar particles off quicker
quiz.why: In warm water, water particles move faster and hit the grains more often. Sugar does not melt in warm water: it would need about 186 degrees Celsius to melt. It dissolves.

quiz.p: Kavya, a girl in Class 3, wants cold lemonade with no sugar at the bottom. What should she do first?
opts: Dissolve the sugar in a little warm water
quiz.why: Sugar dissolves fast in warm water and then stays dissolved when cold water is added. Ice slows dissolving down.

quiz.p: Farhan, a boy in Class 2, pours salt water through a cotton cloth. What comes through?
opts: Plain water, with the salt left on the cloth
quiz.why: Dissolved salt is far smaller than the gaps in the cloth, so it goes through. A cloth catches only things that have not dissolved, like atta or tea leaves.

quiz.p: A tea strainer catches the tea leaves. Why does the tea in the cup still taste of tea?
opts: The taste and colour dissolved in the water and went through
quiz.why: The flavour and colour dissolve in the hot water. The leaves themselves do not, so the strainer catches them.

quiz.p: Divya, a girl in Class 3, tests sugar in cold and in warm water. To make it a fair test, what must stay the same?
opts: The amount of water and sugar, and the stirring
quiz.why: In a fair test, only one thing changes. Here that is the temperature, so everything else stays the same. If the temperature stayed the same, there would be nothing to test.

quiz.p: What did Svante Arrhenius show about salt in water?
opts: It comes apart into charged particles called ions by itself
quiz.why: Arrhenius showed that salt splits into ions as it dissolves, with no electric current needed. His examiners doubted him, but he won the Nobel Prize in 1903.

applications: ORS, oral rehydration solution, is salt and sugar dissolved in clean water. It helps the body take back water lost in diarrhoea.
Sherbets, nannari sarbath, lemonade and payasam all depend on dissolving sugar or jaggery.
Salt pans along the coasts of Tamil Nadu and Gujarat get salt by letting the sun evaporate sea water.
Water purifiers and filters catch dirt, but dissolved salts need other methods, such as boiling down or special membranes.
Doctors make medicines that dissolve, so the body can take them in.
Plants take in minerals only after they have dissolved in the water in the soil.
Washing clothes uses soap and detergent dissolved in water to lift oil and dirt.

open_questions.q: Can we predict how much of a brand new substance will dissolve, just from what its particles are like?
open_questions.why_open: Chemists can measure solubility exactly, but predicting it from scratch is still hard, even with powerful computers.

open_questions.q: Exactly how do water particles arrange themselves around each ion as salt dissolves, moment by moment?
open_questions.why_open: This happens in less than a billionth of a second, and scientists still study it with fast lasers and computer models.

open_questions.q: How did the very first salt get into the oceans, and has the sea always been about as salty as it is now?
open_questions.why_open: Scientists have strong ideas from rocks and old sea water trapped in crystals, but the full story over billions of years is still being worked out.

maths.problem: Three tablespoons of water is about 45 millilitres. A tablespoon is 15 millilitres. How many tablespoons would you need for 90 millilitres, about half a cup?
maths.explain: Each tablespoon is 15 millilitres. 45 millilitres is 3 tablespoons. 90 is twice 45, so it is twice 3, which is 6 tablespoons.
maths.context: This is about measuring water for the Full Glass Test.
maths.why_maths: Knowing how much water you used lets you compare your results with someone else's, or make the test bigger.

maths.problem: Three tablespoons of water dissolved 3 spoons of salt. Lakshmi, a girl in Class 3, doubles the water to 6 tablespoons. How many spoons of salt do you predict it will dissolve? Why?
maths.explain: Twice as much water can dissolve twice as much salt, because each part of the water has the same limit. 3 doubled is 6.
maths.context: This is about predicting a result from the Full Glass Test.
maths.why_maths: Seeing a pattern lets you predict a new result before you test it.

maths.problem: In the Cold, Room or Warm test, cold water took 90 stirs, room water took 45 and warm water took 20. How many times more stirs did cold water take than room water?
maths.explain: 45 plus 45 is 90. So cold water took twice as many stirs as room water. Warm water was more than twice as fast as room water.
maths.context: These are made-up results from the Cold, Room or Warm test.
maths.why_maths: Comparing numbers shows how big the difference really is, not just which one was fastest.

maths.problem: Anjali's lemonade recipe uses 4 tablespoons of sugar for 3 cups of water. She wants to make 9 cups for a party. How much sugar does she need?
maths.explain: 9 cups is 3 lots of 3 cups. Each 3 cups needs 4 tablespoons. 3 lots of 4 is 12 tablespoons.
maths.context: This is about scaling up the lemonade recipe.
maths.why_maths: Scaling a recipe keeps the drink tasting the same, because the sugar and water stay in the same proportion.

maths.problem: Odd one out: in the Full Glass Test, four children, Kavya, Arjun, Priya and Farhan, each did the test. Kavya's salt glass took 3 spoons, Arjun's took 3, Priya's took 2, and Farhan's took 7. Which result looks odd, and what might have gone wrong?
maths.explain: The others are close together, at 2 or 3. Seven is far more. Farhan may have used more water, small spoons that were not level, warm water, or he may have counted cloudy water as grains being gone. Checking how he did it is the way to find out.
maths.context: These are made-up results from four children doing the Full Glass Test.
maths.why_maths: Spotting a result that does not fit the pattern helps you find mistakes in how a test was done.

playtest: Every experiment and activity was walked through as if in a city flat with kitchen things. The Full Glass Test uses three tablespoons of water, about 45 millilitres, so salt runs out at the third or fourth level teaspoon (about 16 grams dissolve) while sugar is still dissolving at ten (about 90 grams would dissolve). Stopping sugar at ten keeps the test under 35 minutes, and the syrup is used again for lemonade. Near the limit salt dissolves slowly, so each spoon is stirred for a full minute, and the parent note says to stir once more before calling it full. Iodised table salt can make water slightly cloudy, so children are told to look for grains on the bottom, not cloudiness. Clear glasses or plastic cups are needed, because steel tumblers hide the bottom. Warm water is only bath-warm and always made by a grown-up. The warm salt test is expected to show almost no difference, which is the point. In the kitchen test, turmeric and tea dust colour the water but mostly settle, which the notes explain. The oil test uses a capped bottle to avoid spills. The coffee activity is optional, for homes that make filter coffee or tea, and the child only watches the hot water. The spine is the intro, the kitchen test, the Full Glass Test, the explanation cards, roots and the quiz, about 80 minutes.
